description: Blues — built on the 12-bar blues form (typically I7-IV7-V7), played with a shuffle or swung eighth-note feel. Drums keep a steady shuffle groove with the snare on 2 and 4; bass usually walks or outlines the chord tones with a simple, repetitive line. Chords lean on dominant 7ths throughout, even on the I chord, for that gritty, unresolved blues colour. The mixolydian mode and the blues scale are the primary melodic vocabulary

Rock — driven by a steady backbeat, with the snare hitting hard on 2 and 4 and drums generally playing straight eighth or quarter notes rather than swung. Bass typically locks tightly to the kick drum, often playing simple root-fifth patterns. Chord progressions favor power chords and simple triads (I-IV-V, I-V-vi-IV), usually major or minor rather than jazz-extended harmony, with an emphasis on rhythmic drive over harmonic complexity

Pop — centers on simple, repetitive chord progressions (especially I-V-vi-IV) that repeat across verse and chorus with minimal variation. Drums keep a clean, steady four-on-the-floor or straightforward backbeat groove; bass usually doubles the chord roots in a simple, supportive pattern rather than an independent melodic line. Chords are typically plain major/minor triads or simple 7ths, prioritizing catchy, singable harmony over complexity

Funk — built around tight, syncopated 16th-note rhythms with a heavy emphasis on the downbeat ("the one"). Bass is the lead voice of the groove, often syncopated and percussive, interlocking tightly with the kick drum rather than just outlining the chord. Drums favor ghost notes and off-beat snare/hi-hat accents over straight patterns. Chords are usually dominant 9ths or minor 7ths, played short and percussive (stabs) rather than sustained, with harmonic movement often staying on a single chord for extended vamps

Reggae — defined by the one-drop drum pattern, where the kick and snare land together on beat 3 and beats 1 is left empty, giving the groove a laid-back, behind-the-beat feel. Guitar or keys play a sharp offbeat "skank" on the upbeats. Bass is the most prominent melodic element, playing a slow, repetitive, often syncopated line that anchors the groove more than the drums do. Chords are typically simple major, minor, or dominant 7th, with progressions that move slowly and repeat over long stretches

Jazz — harmonically built on ii-V-I progressions and extended or altered chords (maj7, min7, dominant 7, and beyond), often with a swung eighth-note feel. Drums typically play a ride-cymbal-led swing pattern rather than a driving backbeat, with the snare and kick used sparingly for accents (comping) rather than steady pulse. Bass walks — a steady quarter-note line outlining chord tones and passing tones through each change — rather than repeating a fixed pattern. Mixolydian, dorian, and harmonic minor are common melodic sources over the moving harmony
